fixes.explanation: That's the one, baker. Moses says the priests "…are to eat the food offerings to the LORD; that is their inheritance." (Deuteronomy 18:1) The whole tribe of Levi has no portion or inheritance with Israel, so those offerings are what Moses names as theirs. That's a different kind of inheritance than the rest of Israel gets.

Manna is a real thing, friend. God told Moses He would rain down bread from heaven for Israel (Exodus 16:4). But that's not what Moses names here. He says the Levites eat the food offerings to the LORD (Deuteronomy 18:1).

Yes, baker! Moses says, "…the LORD is their inheritance, as He promised them." (Deuteronomy 18:2) The Levites have no inheritance among their brothers, but they have Him, and He is the One who promised it. That's an inheritance nobody can come and repossess.

That's right, baker. Moses says, "…the LORD your God has chosen Levi and his sons out of all your tribes to stand and minister in His name for all time." (Deuteronomy 18:5) So the gifts go with the job: standing and ministering in His name. And "for all time" is no short-term contract.

Close in feeling, friend, but that's not the word in the verse. Moses says the LORD has "…chosen Levi and his sons out of all your tribes to stand and minister in His name for all time." (Deuteronomy 18:5) Levi was picked out of all the tribes for a job: to stand and minister in His name. The verse points to the choosing and the service.

Right on, baker. Moses says, "…because of these detestable things, the LORD your God is driving out the nations before you." (Deuteronomy 18:12) Just before that, he lists the things, like divination, sorcery and consulting a medium (Deuteronomy 18:10–11). So the reason is the practices themselves, and Moses names them plainly.

Not this time, friend. Moses says the LORD "…will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers." (Deuteronomy 18:15) That means from among Israel's own people. Egypt's priests aren't mentioned anywhere in that sentence.

Yes, baker. The people said, "Let us not hear the voice of the LORD our God or see this great fire anymore, so that we will not die!" (Deuteronomy 18:16) I think that voice and that fire were more than they could stand. I bet my mustache would have stood straight up.

Good guess, baker, but that's not what they asked here. At Horeb, they said, "Let us not hear the voice of the LORD our God or see this great fire anymore, so that we will not die!" (Deuteronomy 18:16) Their request was about the voice and the fire. Going back to Egypt isn't in it.

I'm glad you checked, friend, because it's the other way around. The LORD said to Moses, "They have spoken well." (Deuteronomy 18:17) Moses doesn't say anything about anger. Then the LORD goes on to promise a prophet (Deuteronomy 18:18). So the statement is false.

Right, baker. The LORD says, "…if any prophet dares to speak a message in My name that I have not commanded him to speak, or to speak in the name of other gods, that prophet must be put to death." (Deuteronomy 18:20) It's a heavy verse, and I think it shows how seriously God takes His words. Two things are named here: speaking in His name what He didn't command, and speaking in the name of other gods.

You got it, baker. Moses says, "When a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD and the message does not come to pass or come true, that is a message the LORD has not spoken." (Deuteronomy 18:22) So a message that never comes true is one the LORD has not spoken. Then Moses adds that the prophet has spoken presumptuously, and tells the people, "Do not be afraid of him."

Interesting thought, baker, but Moses doesn't say a word about tribes here. He says that when a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD and the message "…does not come to pass or come true, that is a message the LORD has not spoken." (Deuteronomy 18:22) The question is what happens to the message. Where the prophet comes from never enters into it.
